label: Réginald Garrigou-Lagrange, O.P, Dieu I, ch: Becoming reading of the inertia bridge: a body…
locator: I, ch. III, n. 36 B, pp. 252, 254: le mouvement local n'est pas plus un état que les autres mouvements, c'est un devenir
interpretation: Garrigou-Lagrange's own thesis against the Cartesian notion of a 'state of motion'. P. 252: one cannot speak of a state of motion, since motion, being essentially a change, is the contrary of a state; there is no less change in the passage from one position to another during the motion than in the passage from rest to motion, so if the first change needs a cause the later ones need one by the same title. P. 254: the Aristotelian definition of becoming, the passage from potency to act, applies to local motion as to qualitative motion and growth; local motion is no more a state than the other motions, it is a becoming. Read as: a body persevering in uniform rectilinear motion is being moved in that respect, in the sense of DEF-MOTION-AS-REDUCTION. The statement is weaker than the source: it covers only uniform motion in which a body perseveres, not all local motion. Garrigou-Lagrange does not draw the inertial objection from it: he denies that a communicated motion continues without cause (pp. 253-254, footnote, citing Poincaré) and holds that the motion of Pure Act, which physics cannot exclude, moves a body perpetuating its motion in the void (Note, pp. 760-761). French original; OCR text of the 1914 first edition.
